subject: Art & Design
title: Cubism: Shattering the Single Viewpoint
description: A micro-lesson that makes Cubism: Shattering the Single Viewpoint usable.

hook.text: Picasso and Braque asked: why paint a face from one angle when you can show all angles at once?

buildup.text: Cubism fractured objects into geometric planes and reassembled them on a flat canvas.

discovery.text: It wasn't about abstraction for its own sake — it was a more complete way of representing reality.

twist.text: Cubism killed the 500-year reign of single-point perspective that started in the Renaissance.

climax.text: It influenced architecture, literature, music, and fashion — not just painting.

punchline.text: They broke the image to show more of the truth.

details.summary: Cubism, developed by Picasso and Braque around 1907, depicted objects from multiple simultaneous viewpoints, fracturing forms into geometric planes. A face might show front and profile views at once.
details.whyItMatters: Cubism destroyed the 500-year-old convention that paintings should show a scene from one fixed viewpoint. It proved that art could represent how we actually experience objects — from multiple angles over time — rather than frozen snapshots.
takeaways: Depicted objects from multiple simultaneous viewpoints
Picasso and Braque developed the movement around 1907
The most revolutionary visual idea since the Renaissance

faq.question: Why do Cubist paintings look so strange?
faq.answer: They show multiple views of an object simultaneously — front, side, top — flattened into a single image. A guitar might show its front, side, and interior strings all at once. This matches how we actually know objects — from accumulated views over time — rather than a single frozen glance.

faq.question: What inspired Picasso and Braque to invent Cubism?
faq.answer: Cézanne's geometric analysis of nature, African and Iberian masks that showed faces as flat geometric planes, and photography's ability to capture reality freeing painting from representational duty. These influences converged in Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907).
